General
1. Which public bodies are in scope of this PPN?
heading_path: 1. Which public bodies are in scope of this PPN?

content_blocks.text: All central government departments, their executive agencies and non-departmental public bodies when awarding public contracts [footnote 1] for goods and/or services and/or works, other than special regime contracts [footnote 2] , as are best value authorities in England within the meaning of section 1 of the Local Government Act 1999 and parish councils in England. Local government specific FAQs are set out in questions 27-34. Other public sector contracting authorities should consider applying the PPN.
heading_path: 1. Which public bodies are in scope of this PPN?

content_blocks.text: 2. Does this policy apply to the Devolved Administrations?
heading_path: 1. Which public bodies are in scope of this PPN?
2. Does this policy apply to the Devolved Administrations?

content_blocks.text: No. The Devolved Administrations will issue separate guidance.
heading_path: 1. Which public bodies are in scope of this PPN?
2. Does this policy apply to the Devolved Administrations?

content_blocks.text: 3. What about UK registered suppliers controlled by a ’Russian or Belarusian supplier’?
heading_path: 1. Which public bodies are in scope of this PPN?
3. What about UK registered suppliers controlled by a ’Russian or Belarusian supplier’?

content_blocks.text: These can be considered as a ’Russian or Belarusian supplier’ when it comes to contract termination. However, for new procurements, in-scope organisations must consider whether the supplier is constituted or organised under the law of Russia or Belarus or their ‘Persons of Significant Control’ or connect persons information states Russia or Belarus as the place of residency. In those cases, you can exclude the supplier from the procurement or decline to consider their bid, providing that supplier (or any member of their supply chain they rely on to deliver the contract) is not a UK supplier or a treaty state supplier.
heading_path: 1. Which public bodies are in scope of this PPN?
3. What about UK registered suppliers controlled by a ’Russian or Belarusian supplier’?

content_blocks.text: Special consideration should be given where the supplier has a more complex group structure involving parent or group companies that are UK or treaty state suppliers.

content_blocks.text: 4. What if my existing supplier has a Russian/Belarusian parent but the supplier’s registered office is in a GPA territory or another country with which the UK has an international agreement on procurement?
heading_path: 1. Which public bodies are in scope of this PPN?

4. What if my existing supplier has a Russian/Belarusian parent but the supplier’s registered office is in a GPA territory or another country with which the UK has an international agreement on procurement?

content_blocks.text: This would be classed as a Russian/Belarusian supplier for contract termination. However, for new procurements, special consideration should be given where the supplier has a more complex group structure, such as a parent or group companies that are UK or treaty state suppliers.

5. Is Russia or Belarus a member of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) Agreement on Government Procurement (GPA)?

content_blocks.text: No, neither Russia or Belarus are members of GPA and the UK does not have any international agreements containing procurement obligations with either country.

6. What sectors are Russian/Belarusian suppliers active in?

content_blocks.text: Several sectors including oil and gas. However, it should not be assumed they are not involved in other sectors.

content_blocks.text: 7. What reason should I give to the Contractor as to why I am terminating the contract?
heading_path: 1. Which public bodies are in scope of this PPN?
7. What reason should I give to the Contractor as to why I am terminating the contract?

content_blocks.text: The prime contractor should be advised that its contract is being terminated in response to the situation in Ukraine and the resulting sanctions.
heading_path: 1. Which public bodies are in scope of this PPN?
7. What reason should I give to the Contractor as to why I am terminating the contract?

content_blocks.text: Existing contracts
8. Do I have to terminate all in-scope contracts?
heading_path: 8. Do I have to terminate all in-scope contracts?

content_blocks.text: There is no central policy mandate to terminate any contracts with Russian/Belarusian prime contractors. The UK government has made a statement which calls on relevant contracting authorities to exit relevant contracts at their earliest convenience, but the decision whether or not to terminate a relevant contract lies with individual contracting authorities. There may be valid financial, operational, national security, or commercial reasons why a contract cannot or should not be terminated.
heading_path: 8. Do I have to terminate all in-scope contracts?

content_blocks.text: 9. Should I terminate my contracts with Russian/Belarusian suppliers now?
heading_path: 9. Should I terminate my contracts with Russian/Belarusian suppliers now?

content_blocks.text: Contracting authorities should consider each contract individually, bearing in mind its criticality, risk profile, value, and the availability and cost of alternative supply, as well as whether the terms of the contract allow termination at will, and the likelihood of any financial penalties or other liabilities, such as intellectual property implications, before making a decision. You should seek legal advice where necessary.
heading_path: 9. Should I terminate my contracts with Russian/Belarusian suppliers now?

content_blocks.text: 10. Which clauses in my contract can be used to terminate my contract if there are no other performance issues?
heading_path: 10. Which clauses in my contract can be used to terminate my contract if there are no other performance issues?

content_blocks.text: We would expect contracts to contain clear termination clauses. These might offer termination with or without notice but without a cost to the contracting authority, e.g. in the form of a break clause, or with notice for convenience, which describes how any
heading_path: 10. Which clauses in my contract can be used to terminate my contract if there are no other performance issues?

content_blocks.text: payments due are calculated. You must ascertain and assess the consequences of terminating the contract, particularly the cost to the contracting authority, before a decision to terminate is made.
heading_path: 10. Which clauses in my contract can be used to terminate my contract if there are no other performance issues?

content_blocks.text: 11. My contract requires me to give 90 days notice of termination? What should I do?
heading_path: 11. My contract requires me to give 90 days notice of termination? What should I do?

content_blocks.text: Notice to terminate should be given in accordance with the terms of the contract. Where a decision is made to terminate a contract, as a guide, the contracting authority should take the termination option which results in the lowest overall payment to the prime contractor, from a whole life cost perspective. The financial implications of terminating the contract and the impact of different notice periods, and supplier switching costs, should be carefully assessed.
heading_path: 11. My contract requires me to give 90 days notice of termination? What should I do?

content_blocks.text: 12. Will I incur financial penalties for terminating my contract?
heading_path: 12. Will I incur financial penalties for terminating my contract?

content_blocks.text: This depends entirely on the terms of the contract. You should consider each contract individually and check whether it allows for termination at will/convenience and whether this will incur any financial penalties. If the termination will incur additional costs, these will need to be covered by the existing budgets.
heading_path: 12. Will I incur financial penalties for terminating my contract?

content_blocks.text: 13. Where might terminating a contract benefit a supplier?
heading_path: 13. Where might terminating a contract benefit a supplier?

content_blocks.text: There could be a scenario where it is better to not terminate the contract because the supplier would considerably benefit. For example, a customer might have secured a fixed three-year contract with lower prices than those prevailing in the market at the proposed point of termination. If the customer terminates the contract, the supplier can now sell their energy at a higher rate. Meanwhile, the previous customer might secure a contract with a different supplier but this too is at the higher market rate.
heading_path: 13. Where might terminating a contract benefit a supplier?

content_blocks.text: 14. What about subcontractors?

Where you identify subcontractors that are Russian or Belarusian suppliers you should start to understand their impact on your supply chain and discuss with your prime contractor their links to Russia or Belarus. There is no requirement at this stage to consider the termination of subcontracts with Russian or Belarusian subcontractors.
15. How do I know if I have Russian/Belarusian suppliers in the supply chain?
heading_path: 15. How do I know if I have Russian/Belarusian suppliers in the supply chain?

content_blocks.text: Prime contractors should identify their main subcontractors (i.e. those being relied on to deliver the contract) when bidding for the contract so this information should be available to you, for example, this information should normally be have been have been captured as part of the information the supplier uploaded to Supplier’s Basic Information on the central digital platform. Supply chain mapping can help to identify those suppliers involved in the supply chain, to source (if necessary) to identify risks. The Companies House Register may be a useful information source.
heading_path: 15. How do I know if I have Russian/Belarusian suppliers in the supply chain?

content_blocks.text: 16. My contract is via a Framework Agreement - how do I access information relating to the supply chain?
heading_path: 16. My contract is via a Framework Agreement - how do I access information relating to the supply chain?

content_blocks.text: You should contact the Framework Agreement owner to request the information if you are not able to get it from your supplier directly. Where your contract is via a Crown Commercial Service (CCS) commercial agreement, you should contact the helpdesk
heading_path: 16. My contract is via a Framework Agreement - how do I access information relating to the supply chain?

content_blocks.text: on 0345 410 2222 or info@crowncommercial.gov.uk . For other public buying organisations you should contact them directly.
heading_path: 16. My contract is via a Framework Agreement - how do I access information relating to the supply chain?

content_blocks.text: 17. Should I map my supply chain to ascertain the risks? / What is supply chain mapping?
heading_path: 17. Should I map my supply chain to ascertain the risks? / What is supply chain mapping?

content_blocks.text: It should not be necessary to undertake full supply chain mapping to source, to execute the actions set out in this PPN. However, you should ensure you have sufficient information on which to identify and assess the risks effectively.
heading_path: 17. Should I map my supply chain to ascertain the risks? / What is supply chain mapping?

content_blocks.text: Mapping your supply chain means gathering information about your suppliers, their own suppliers, and the people who work in your supply chain to create a global map of your supply network. Its primary function is to identify and manage risk at all levels of the supply chain. Supply chain mapping involves working collaboratively with your prime contractor to gather data on subsequent tiers to manage risks particularly where a supplier is unable to deliver or has become unreliable as a result of sanctions, inability to travel or other disruptions.
heading_path: 17. Should I map my supply chain to ascertain the risks? / What is supply chain mapping?

content_blocks.text: 18. Who should I consult if I am unsure whether to recommend termination?
heading_path: 18. Who should I consult if I am unsure whether to recommend termination?

content_blocks.text: The decision as to whether to terminate a contract is for the contracting authority to make. Legal, financial and commercial advice will assist decision making.
heading_path: 18. Who should I consult if I am unsure whether to recommend termination?

content_blocks.text: 19. Who should make the decision to terminate the contract?
heading_path: 19. Who should make the decision to terminate the contract?

content_blocks.text: The decision whether to terminate a contract is for each contracting authority to make. Recommendations to terminate should be well-documented and be approved by your commercial director and accounting officer (or their equivalents in other parts of the public sector). If the termination is contentious, central government departments should seek approval from their Permanent Secretary.
heading_path: 19. Who should make the decision to terminate the contract?

content_blocks.text: 20. What if the contract I want to terminate is critical / there are no alternative suppliers?
heading_path: 20. What if the contract I want to terminate is critical / there are no alternative suppliers?

content_blocks.text: You should always carefully consider the risks associated with terminating a contract before taking any action. Critical contracts should not be terminated before there is a suitable alternative solution available that can be implemented without incurring disproportionate costs. Contracts with no alternative source of supply should not be terminated unless the contracting authority is assured the risk in doing so is manageable.
heading_path: 20. What if the contract I want to terminate is critical / there are no alternative suppliers?

content_blocks.text: New contracts
21. Can I let a new contract to a Russian/Belarusian supplier?
heading_path: 21. Can I let a new contract to a Russian/Belarusian supplier?

content_blocks.text: It is possible to not consider Russian or Belarusian suppliers in new procurements in certain cases. Suppliers who are constituted or organised under the law of Russia or Belarus or their ‘Persons of Significant Control’ information states Russia or Belarus as the place of residency can be excluded, as long as the supplier or any member of their supply chain they rely on to deliver the contract is not a UK or a treaty state supplier.
heading_path: 21. Can I let a new contract to a Russian/Belarusian supplier?

content_blocks.text: If either of these two criteria are met, the supplier should not be automatically excluded from a new procurement, as non-discrimination provisions of the Procurement Act 2023 will apply. Where the supplier has a more complex group structure involving parent or group companies that are UK or treaty state suppliers, you should consider the specific circumstances and take legal advice where appropriate.
heading_path: 21. Can I let a new contract to a Russian/Belarusian supplier?

content_blocks.text: 22. Do I have to check whether an exclusion ground applies?
heading_path: 22. Do I have to check whether an exclusion ground applies?

content_blocks.text: Excluding a supplier from a procurement in this context does not rely on the exclusion grounds in the Procurement Act 2023. It is not necessary to consider these exclusion grounds since there is no obligation under the Procurement Act 2023 to consider non- treaty state, such as Russian or Belarusian, suppliers.
heading_path: 22. Do I have to check whether an exclusion ground applies?

content_blocks.text: You must however check for the absence of exclusion grounds in accordance with sections 26 and 27 of the Procurement Act 2023 as a matter of normal practice.
heading_path: 22. Do I have to check whether an exclusion ground applies?

content_blocks.text: 23. How do I treat a Russian/Belarusian supplier who has submitted a bid for a new contract?
heading_path: 23. How do I treat a Russian/Belarusian supplier who has submitted a bid for a new contract?

content_blocks.text: It is possible to decline to consider bids from Russian or Belarusian suppliers in certain circumstances. For suppliers who are constituted or organised under the law of Russia or Belarus or their ‘Persons of Significant Control’ information states Russia or Belarus as the place of residency, the supplier’s bid can be discounted as long as the supplier or any member of their supply chain they rely on to deliver the contract It is possible to decline to consider bids from Russian or Belarusian suppliers in certain circumstances. For suppliers who are constituted or organised under the law of Russia or Belarus or their ‘Persons of Significant Control’ information states Russia or Belarus as the place of residency, the supplier’s bid can be discounted as long as the supplier or any member of their supply chain they rely on to deliver the contract is not a UK or a treaty state supplier.
heading_path: 23. How do I treat a Russian/Belarusian supplier who has submitted a bid for a new contract?

content_blocks.text: If either of these two criteria are met, the supplier should not be automatically excluded from a new procurement, as the Procurement Act 2023 will apply. Where the supplier has a more complex group structure involving parent or group companies that are UK or treaty state suppliers, you should consider the specific circumstances and take legal advice where appropriate.
heading_path: 23. How do I treat a Russian/Belarusian supplier who has submitted a bid for a new contract?

content_blocks.text: 24. How do I confirm if a bidder is Russian/Belarusian?
heading_path: 24. How do I confirm if a bidder is Russian/Belarusian?

content_blocks.text: In most cases, this information should normally be captured as part of the information the supplier uploads to the Supplier’s Basic Information on the central digital platform. It will also require them to set out details of their supply chain and their Persons of Significant Control (i.e. beneficial owner). You can use this information to validate whether or not they are Russian/Belarusian.
heading_path: 24. How do I confirm if a bidder is Russian/Belarusian?

content_blocks.text: 25. What is a Person of Significant Control?
heading_path: 25. What is a Person of Significant Control?

content_blocks.text: A person with significant control (PSC) is someone who owns or controls a company. They are sometimes called ‘beneficial owners’. UK registered companies must identify their PSCs and tell Companies House who they are. A company can have one or more PSCs. Most PSCs are those who hold:
heading_path: 25. What is a Person of Significant Control?

content_blocks.text: more than 25% of shares in the company;
heading_path: 25. What is a Person of Significant Control?

content_blocks.text: more than 25% of voting rights in the company; or
heading_path: 25. What is a Person of Significant Control?

content_blocks.text: the right to appoint or remove the majority of the board of directors.
heading_path: 25. What is a Person of Significant Control?

content_blocks.text: A PSC might influence or control a company through other means. This could be directly, or on behalf of someone else. For example, someone may influence or control the actions of directors or shareholders. This condition will only apply in limited circumstances. The full PSC guidance has more information on the meaning of ‘significant influence or control’.
heading_path: 25. What is a Person of Significant Control?

content_blocks.text: If a company is controlled by a trust or firm without ‘legal personality’:- This condition will only apply in limited circumstances. If a trust or firm meets any nature of control, all trustees or members/partners of the firm should be recorded as PSCs of the company and this information registered at Companies House.
heading_path: 25. What is a Person of Significant Control?

content_blocks.text: 26. How do I verify the information I receive?
heading_path: 26. How do I verify the information I receive?

content_blocks.text: You should conduct due diligence in the usual way to check supplier details, for example from the Companies House Register and other open information sources, or seek verification directly from the supplier.
heading_path: 26. How do I verify the information I receive?

content_blocks.text: Local government specific FAQs
27. What is Section 17 of the Local Government Act 1988?
heading_path: 27. What is Section 17 of the Local Government Act 1988?

content_blocks.text: Contracting Authorities subject to section 17 of the Local Government Act 1988 should note that in general they are prohibited from taking into account non-commercial considerations in procurement decisions.
heading_path: 27. What is Section 17 of the Local Government Act 1988?

content_blocks.text: However, Local Government (Exclusion of Non-Commercial Considerations)(England) Order 2022 ) (“the 2022 Order”) came into force on 1 July 2022 to enable best value authorities and parish councils to apply this PPN.
heading_path: 27. What is Section 17 of the Local Government Act 1988?

content_blocks.text: 28. Are local government contracting authorities required to review their contract portfolio as set out in this PPN?
heading_path: 28. Are local government contracting authorities required to review their contract portfolio as set out in this PPN?

content_blocks.text: No. Best value authorities and parish councils should consider whether it is proportionate to conduct a risk assessment and review of contract portfolios bearing in mind resource implications and take action accordingly.
heading_path: 28. Are local government contracting authorities required to review their contract portfolio as set out in this PPN?

content_blocks.text: 29. Can local government contracting authorities terminate contracts for commercial reasons?
heading_path: 29. Can local government contracting authorities terminate contracts for commercial reasons?

content_blocks.text: Local authorities are subject to section 17 of the Local Government Act 1988 (listed in Schedule 2 to the Act) and with regard to their procurement functions may not take into account ‘non-commercial considerations’ in deciding whether to terminate existing contracts or letting new contracts. This includes for reasons relating to the location or country of origin of a supplier.
heading_path: 29. Can local government contracting authorities terminate contracts for commercial reasons?

content_blocks.text: In response to the invasion of Ukraine, the Government brought forward the Local Government (Exclusion of Non-Commercial Considerations) (England) Order 2022.
heading_path: 29. Can local government contracting authorities terminate contracts for commercial reasons?

content_blocks.text: This Order provides that, for best value authorities and parish councils in England, the country or territory of origin of entities (both suppliers and subcontractors) with which these organisations hold public supply or works contracts can be taken into consideration where either:
heading_path: 29. Can local government contracting authorities terminate contracts for commercial reasons?

content_blocks.text: the country or territory of origin of supplies to the contractor is the Russian Federation or the Republic of Belarus, or
heading_path: 29. Can local government contracting authorities terminate contracts for commercial reasons?

content_blocks.text: the location of the business activities or interests of a contractor is the Russian Federation or the Republic of Belarus. [footnote 3]
heading_path: 29. Can local government contracting authorities terminate contracts for commercial reasons?

content_blocks.text: This could include entities which are constituted or organised under the law of Russia or Belarus, or whose ‘Persons of Significant Control’ information states Russia or Belarus as the place of residency. However, during new procurements best value authorities and parish councils must also pay careful attention to entities registered in the UK or those which have significant business operations in the UK (or a country to which the UK has a relevant international agreement) but are controlled by entities in Russia or Belarus.
heading_path: 29. Can local government contracting authorities terminate contracts for commercial reasons?

content_blocks.text: 30. What are the Best Value considerations that local government should take into account in relation to this PPN?
heading_path: 30. What are the Best Value considerations that local government should take into account in relation to this PPN?

content_blocks.text: Local authorities have a Best Value Duty under section 3 of the Local Government Act 1999, which is a duty to secure continuous improvement in the exercise of their functions, having regard to economy, efficiency and effectiveness. Generally, terminating contracts for non-commercial reasons, or paying any significant termination charges, or terminating contracts for a more expensive alternative, could be incompatible with the Best Value Duty, depending on the contractual arrangements and the circumstances.
heading_path: 30. What are the Best Value considerations that local government should take into account in relation to this PPN?

content_blocks.text: However, the changes made by the 2022 Order enable best value authorities and parish councils in England to apply this PPN.
heading_path: 30. What are the Best Value considerations that local government should take into account in relation to this PPN?

content_blocks.text: 31. Will local government’s social value considerations apply to this PPN?
heading_path: 31. Will local government’s social value considerations apply to this PPN?

content_blocks.text: Section 1 of the Public Services (Social Value) Act 2012 requires local authorities to consider how they might use their procurement to improve the economic, social and environmental wellbeing of their local area. This applies only at the pre-procurement stage and so should be considered for new procurements if existing arrangements are due to expire, but does not apply to contract termination.
heading_path: 31. Will local government’s social value considerations apply to this PPN?

content_blocks.text: 32. Does the 2022 Order also cover contracts let under framework agreements?
heading_path: 32. Does the 2022 Order also cover contracts let under framework agreements?

content_blocks.text: Yes. The 2022 Order disapplies Section 17(5)(e) of the Local Government Act 1988 for these entities. As such it applies to all ‘procurement functions’, which includes functions relating to proposed or subsisting contracts for public supply, services or works and also applies to call offs from Framework Agreements.
heading_path: 32. Does the 2022 Order also cover contracts let under framework agreements?

content_blocks.text: 33. The Local Government Act 1988 refers to subcontractors, supplier, associated bodies and customers of the contractor – should best value authorities and parish councils prioritise their consideration of any of these?
heading_path: 33. The Local Government Act 1988 refers to subcontractors, supplier, associated bodies and customers of the contractor – should best value authorities and parish councils prioritise their consideration of any of these?

content_blocks.text: Council leaders have expressed a clear desire to cut ties with companies backed by, or linked to, the Russian and Belarusian state regimes, while minimising the impact to taxpayers and the delivery of public services. Identifying contracts with Russian or Belarusian contractors is a probable first step and such activity is for each body to determine individually. Best value authorities and parish councils will need to consider the resource implications associated with undertaking such a review and whether it is proportionate to also review the subcontractors, suppliers, associated bodies and customers of their contractors.
heading_path: 33. The Local Government Act 1988 refers to subcontractors, supplier, associated bodies and customers of the contractor – should best value authorities and parish councils prioritise their consideration of any of these?

content_blocks.text: 34. Should best value authorities and parish councils terminate contracts with suppliers which have a significant Russian or Belarusian customer base?
heading_path: 34. Should best value authorities and parish councils terminate contracts with suppliers which have a significant Russian or Belarusian customer base?

content_blocks.text: The new legislation disapplies Section 17(5)(e) of the Local Government Act 1988, enabling best value authorities and parish councils to consider the country or territory of origin of supplies to the contractor or the location of the business activities or interests of a contractor, where this is the Russian Federation or the Republic of Belarus. This also applies to a supplier or customer of the contractor; a sub-contractor of the contractor or his supplier or customer; an associated body of the contractor or his supplier or customer; or a sub-contractor of an associated body of the contractor or his supplier or customer.
heading_path: 34. Should best value authorities and parish councils terminate contracts with suppliers which have a significant Russian or Belarusian customer base?

content_blocks.text: As such the 2022 Order also enables best value authorities and parish councils to consider whether a customer of a contractor is the Russian Federation or the Republic of Belarus, in line with the guidance set out in this PPN, and if it is accordingly appropriate to terminate the contracts.
